food.text: Potatoes entered German cuisine in the late 17th century. Rulers such as Frederick the Great promoted them in the 18th century through the Potato Edict, and by the 19th century they were almost everywhere on German tables.

The pierogi recipe dates back to at least 1682, when Poland's first cookbook, Compendium ferculorum, albo Zebranie potraw, was published. These filled dumplings, made by wrapping unleavened dough around a filling and boiling it, became a traditional Polish dish.

From the 16th century, international trade made spices and exotic food items from Asia and South America available in Germany. They were soon incorporated into civic kitchens, the cooking of the towns.
Cookbooks from the 17th century describe pierogi as a staple of the Polish diet. Each holiday had its own special kind of pierogi, and they came in different shapes, fillings and cooking methods.

Traditionally considered peasant food, pierogi eventually spread through all social classes, including the nobility. Their popularity was not limited to the poor, and 17th-century cookbooks record them as part of Polish eating.

Important events such as weddings had their own special type of pierogi, called kurniki, a baked pie filled with chicken. Other pierogi were made especially for mournings or wakes, and some for the caroling season in January.
The use of horseradish in Germany has been documented to the 16th century. It was used as a medicine and as a food, and its leaves were eaten as a vegetable.

art.text: The German Renaissance developed in rather different directions from the Italian Renaissance. It was at first dominated by the central figure of Albrecht Dürer and by the early German lead in printing.

Dürer died in 1528, before it was clear that the Reformation split had become permanent. His pupils could not avoid taking sides. Most leading German artists became Protestants, which cost them most religious commissions, previously the mainstay of artists' revenue.
In Catholic parts of South Germany, the Gothic tradition of wood carving kept flourishing until the end of the 18th century. Carvers adapted it to the changes in style over the centuries.

In the 17th century, bulbous domes became popular in Central Germany, Southern Germany and Austria, and later influenced Poland and Eastern Europe in the Baroque period. Onion spires are especially common on Bavarian country churches. Onion domes on Bavarian pilgrimage churches may show influence from Prague.
The final phase of the Renaissance, Northern Mannerism, was centred around the edges of the German lands. Its centres were Flanders and the Imperial capital of Prague.

Lucas Cranach the Elder, a close friend of Martin Luther, painted a number of "Lutheran altarpieces". Most showed the Last Supper, and some gave the Twelve Apostles the portraits of leading Protestant divines.

Veit Stoss, Tilman Riemenschneider and Peter Vischer the Elder were contemporaries of Dürer. Their long careers covered the transition from the Gothic to the Renaissance period. Their ornament often stayed Gothic even after their compositions began to reflect Renaissance principles.
Martin Luther objected to much Catholic imagery, but not to imagery itself. That is why his friend Cranach could paint Lutheran altarpieces. Even so, this phase of Lutheran art was over before 1550.
Lutheran art probably ended under the more fiercely aniconic influence of Calvinism. Religious works for public display virtually ceased to be produced in Protestant areas.

German art had virtually ceased developing by about 1550, but artists in the preceding decades were very fertile in finding subjects to fill the gap in their order books. Lucas Cranach the Younger, apart from portraits, developed thin vertical pictures of provocative nudes. He gave them classical or Biblical titles.

war.text: The Thirty Years' War, fought mainly in Central Europe between 1618 and 1648, was one of the most destructive conflicts in European history. An estimated 4.5 to 8 million soldiers and civilians died from battle, famine or disease, the vast majority of them civilians. Local returns show only 3% of civilian deaths came from military action; the rest came mainly from bubonic plague (64%), starvation (12%), dysentery (5%) and typhus (4%). Some parts of Germany reported population declines of more than 50%, and reports from the famine years tell of people eating grass or resorting to cannibalism.

The German Peasants' War of 1524 to 1525 was Europe's largest and most widespread popular uprising before the French Revolution in 1789. It failed because of intense opposition from the aristocracy, who slaughtered up to 100,000 of the 300,000 poorly armed peasants and farmers. The survivors were fined and achieved few of their goals. Martin Luther urged the nobles to kill the rebels like mad dogs, writing that they 'must be sliced, choked, stabbed'.

The Battle of Vienna took place at Kahlenberg Mountain on 12 September 1683, after the Ottoman Empire had besieged the city for two months. The Holy Roman Empire and the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth won, under the command of Polish King John III Sobieski. The Ottomans lost around 15,000 dead in the battle according to Podhorodecki, or 8,000 to 15,000 dead and 5,000 to 10,000 captured according to Tucker, on top of at least 20,000 lost during the siege, while the relief force suffered about 3,500 dead and wounded. The Viennese garrison and civilians lost about half their number to all causes during the siege, and the Ottomans would gain no further ground in Europe and never again challenged Vienna.

Prussia's Frederick the Great attacked Austria after Emperor Charles VI died in 1740, invading Silesia in the First Silesian War (1740 to 1742). In the Treaty of Berlin in 1742, Prussia acquired nearly all of Silesia. The victory weakened Austria's prestige and gave Prussia effective equality with Austria within the Holy Roman Empire.
war.source_title: Germany in the early modern period

war.text: The peasants of 1525 faced insurmountable obstacles. Their democratic movement left them without a command structure, they lacked artillery and cavalry, and few had any military experience. Their opponents had experienced military leaders, well-equipped and disciplined armies, and ample funding. The results were massacres: at Frankenhausen most of the insurgents were slain, with estimates of 3,000 to 10,000 dead against as few as six Landsknecht casualties, and at Königshofen the soldiers found about 500 peasants who had feigned death.

The Army of the Holy Roman Empire, the Reichsarmee, was not a standing army. It was mustered only when danger arose and could be deployed only with the consent of the Imperial Diet. It should not be confused with the Imperial Army of the Emperor, which the Habsburgs raised mostly from their own lands.
war.source_title: Army of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: Ottoman preparations for the 1683 siege of Vienna were extensive. Under Grand Vizier Kara Mustafa Pasha, the Ottomans repaired roads and bridges into the Holy Roman Empire and forwarded ammunition and cannons to logistical centers. Ernst Rüdiger von Starhemberg led the Viennese garrison, while Sobieski led the relief forces. Starhemberg refused to surrender after hearing of the massacre at Perchtoldsdorf, where the Ottomans had promised to spare the villagers who surrendered but killed the men and enslaved the women and children, and he ordered any soldier found asleep on watch to be shot.

Thomas Müntzer led the rebel army in the Battle of Frankenhausen on 15 May 1525, after returning to Saxony and Thuringia. Viewing the uprising as an apocalyptic act of God, he styled himself 'God's Servant against the Godless'. The princes' troops broke a truce and attacked; the caught-off-guard peasants fled in panic and most were slain in a massacre, with estimates of 3,000 to 10,000 dead against as few as six Landsknecht casualties. Müntzer was captured, tortured and executed at Mühlhausen on 27 May.

On 23 and 24 June 1525, rebellious peasant bands in the Palatine Peasants' War were decisively defeated at the Battle of Pfeddersheim. By September 1525 all fighting and punitive action had ended. Emperor Charles V and Pope Clement VII thanked the Swabian League for its intervention. Across the war thousands of peasants had been killed, up to 100,000 by the article's account, and the loss of labour devastated the regions' economies for a generation or two.
Contrary to popular belief, the Army of the Empire did not take part in the Thirty Years' War. The Emperor fought that war with the Imperial Army instead.
war.source_title: Army of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: In the Thirty Years' War, the population of Augsburg fell from 48,000 to 21,000 between 1620 and 1650. Munich's fell from 22,000 to 17,000 over the same years. Although some towns may have overstated their losses to avoid taxes, individual records confirm serious declines. The article ties the high mortality to mercenaries who were often unpaid and had to live off the land, and to atrocities such as the destruction of Magdeburg, which created large numbers of refugees who were extremely susceptible to sickness and hunger.

Contrary to popular belief, the Army of the Empire, the Reichsarmee, did not fight in the Thirty Years' War. The Emperor took part with his own Imperial Army instead. The Reichsarmee was not a standing army and could only be deployed with the consent of the Imperial Diet.
war.source_title: Army of the Holy Roman Empire

war.text: In 1695 the Holy Roman Empire had over 280,000 soldiers in the field, yet only 41,300 came from the circle system of the Reichsarmee. Another 93,000 were Imperial Army troops, and Brandenburg-Prussians numbered 21,000. Brandenburg, Bavaria, Saxony and the Palatinate each kept independent armies of 10,000 to 20,000 troops.
war.source_title: Army of the Holy Roman Empire

literature.text: The Baroque period, running from 1600 to 1720, was one of the most fertile times in German literature. Many writers reflected the horrible experiences of the Thirty Years' War in poetry and prose, and the tragedies of Andreas Gryphius and Daniel Caspar von Lohenstein were frequently quite violent. Modern literature in German is said to begin with the authors of the Enlightenment, such as Herder. Later, German Romanticism became the dominant movement of the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

The 18th century golden age of Swiss literature was tied to the influence of French refugees who came to Switzerland after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685. This period is called the "golden age" for Swiss literature. Basel, Bern and especially Zürich were its chief literary centres.

In 1744, the amateur astronomer Eberhard Christian Kindermann imagined a journey to the first moon of Mars in a short story. It is generally considered the first German-language science fiction story. It paid close attention to technical detail, including a calculation of the distance between Mars and Earth.

Goethe's best-selling The Sorrows of Young Werther appeared in 1774 and ended the Sensibility movement of the 1750s to 1770s. Goethe and Friedrich Schiller then led the Sturm und Drang and Weimar Classicism movements.
Louis Bourguet, a French refugee who lived from 1678 to 1743, wrote geological works and founded two periodicals. These brought Italian research and works by French Swiss authors to the country.

Isaak Iselin of Basel, who lived from 1728 to 1782, was considered its chief literary glory. He was one of the founders of the Helvetic Society in 1760 and of the Economical Society in 1777. He wrote about the philosophy of history, ideal politics and economics.

Abraham Ruchat, who lived from 1678 to 1750, wrote an excellent guide-book to Switzerland under the pen-name Gottlieb Kypseler. It was published from 1714 until 1778, and he also appeared in the periodicals founded by Louis Bourguet.

Kindermann's 1744 story was written in the style of the late Baroque period, with allegories drawn from Greco-Roman mythology, such as the appearance of Pheme or the god Bellona. Its Mars is presented as a religious utopia where Martians communicate directly with God, without the intercession of the Bible.

French refugees who came to Switzerland after the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 helped make the 18th century a golden age for Swiss literature. One refugee at Lausanne, Jean Barbeyrac, published a translation of Samuel von Pufendorf's works on natural law in 1712.

In 1557 the German scholar Hieronymus Wolf published his Corpus Historiæ Byzantinæ, a collection of historical sources about the Eastern Empire. The word Byzantium had hardly been used since Constantine renamed the city Constantinople in 330, and Wolf's work gave it its new meaning. French Jesuits and Du Cange later helped entrench the label.
Kindermann's story used Francesco Lana-Terzi's theory of vacuum, dated 1670, to move an aerostat through space. The five travelers of the tale journeyed aboard this craft to the Upper World.

Near the end of the eighteenth century, the German writer Jean Paul wrote a short story called Der Maschinenmensch, or The Man-Machine. It parodied the possible mechanization of all human actions, such as waking up, chewing and writing. It also mocked the materialistic approach of La Mettrie, who had published his treatise in 1747.

science.text: In 1507 the cartographers Martin Waldseemüller and Matthias Ringmann created the first world map on which the land masses in the west of the Atlantic Ocean were named 'America', after Amerigo Vespucci. The Waldseemüller map of 1507 has been part of the UNESCO World Documentary Heritage since 2005.

Johannes Kepler (1571–1630) was one of the originators of the Scientific Revolution of the 16th and 17th centuries, working as an astronomer, physicist, mathematician and natural philosopher. He advocated a heliocentric model of the Solar System, an idea that can be traced back to Aristarchus of Samos and to Nicolaus Copernicus.

The German polymath and philosopher Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz (1646–1716) was a contemporary and competitor of Isaac Newton (1642–1727). The Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Prize, named after him, is one of the highest endowed research prizes in the world.

In March 1600, Kepler became assistant to the astronomer Tycho Brahe at the court of Emperor Rudolf II in Prague, Kingdom of Bohemia. After Brahe's death in October of the next year, Kepler succeeded him as imperial mathematician and court astronomer, a post he held until 1627.

Nicolaus Copernicus's main work, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium, about the heliocentric model, was first published in 1543 in the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg. Its publishers were Johannes Petreius and, likely, the polymath Johannes Schöner.

The Kaiserliche Reichspost, the postal service of the Holy Roman Empire founded in 1490, is often considered the world's first modern postal service. On January 18, 1505, Philip unified communication between Germany, the Netherlands, France and Spain by adding stations in Granada, Toledo, Blois, Paris and Lyon.

In 1755, the philosopher Immanuel Kant published a History of Nature and Theory of Heaven, inspired by Isaac Newton's new theories. He argued that the planets of the Solar System are all necessarily inhabited to allow the migration of souls. This thesis paved the way for interplanetary encounters in fiction.
tags: History of Nature and Theory of Heaven

science.text: The Prussian Academy of Sciences was founded as the Brandenburg Society of Sciences in 1700 by Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. Its successor, the German Academy of Sciences at Berlin, was re-established on July 1, 1946, which was Leibniz's 300th birthday.
science.source_title: German Academy of Sciences at Berlin

science.text: A contract of 1516 gave the Taxis company the right to carry mail and keep the profit, as long as it guaranteed delivery of court mail at defined speeds. Post riders had to fill in time sheets along the way, and in return imperial privileges exempted the company from local taxes, local jurisdiction and military service.

politics.text: Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses of 1517, published in Wittenberg, are usually taken as the start of the Reformation. It divided the German states along religious lines, with the north, the east, and cities such as Strasbourg, Frankfurt, and Nuremberg becoming Protestant, while the south and west largely stayed Catholic. The Reformation led to unprecedented levels of violence and political upheaval in the region.
politics.source_title: Germany in the early modern period

politics.text: By the 18th century, contemporaries widely called the Holy Roman Empire a highly irregular and even sick monarchy. It had no central standing army and no central treasury, and its monarchs were formally elected rather than hereditary.
politics.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: The Habsburg emperor Charles VI failed to produce a male heir, so by the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 he bequeathed his lands to his daughter Maria Theresa. After his death in 1740, the Prussian king Frederick the Great attacked Austria and invaded Silesia. In the Treaty of Berlin of 1742, Prussia gained nearly all of Silesia.
politics.source_title: Germany in the early modern period

politics.text: The Thirty Years' War of 1618 to 1648 ended with the Peace of Westphalia. The Peace of Augsburg of 1555 and other compromises meant to keep the Holy Roman Empire stable had fallen short of preventing it. Fought mostly by mercenary armies, the war destroyed entire regions, which the foraging armies stripped bare. Episodes of famine and disease significantly reduced the population of the German states, the Low Countries and Italy.
politics.source_title: Germany in the early modern period

politics.text: In 1500, Emperor Maximilian agreed to create the Reichsregiment, a central imperial government of twenty members including the Electors. It first met in 1501 in Nuremberg. Maximilian resented it and the Estates failed to support it, so it proved weak and its power returned to Maximilian in 1502.

The Imperial Diet of Constance opened on 27 April 1507. It recognized the unity of the Holy Roman Empire and founded the Imperial Chamber, the empire's supreme court. Later, from 1663, the Diet sat permanently at Regensburg.
Suleiman the Magnificent laid siege to Vienna in 1529 but failed to take the city. In 1532 he made another attack on Vienna, but was repulsed in the siege of Güns.

After the Elector of Saxony converted to Catholicism in 1697 so he could become King of Poland, his electorate stayed officially Protestant. Saxony kept the directorship of the Protestant body. When the Elector's son also converted, Prussia and Hanover tried to take over the directorship in 1717 to 1720 but failed.

In 1692, a new Protestant electoral post was created for the Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, who became known as the Elector of Hanover. This followed the disruption of 1685, when a Catholic branch of the Wittelsbach family inherited the Palatinate. The Imperial Diet officially confirmed the new electorate in 1708.

When Maria Theresa's husband was made Emperor Francis I, she burst out laughing on seeing him in his coronation robes. She regarded the coronation as Kasperltheater, a Punch and Judy show. She herself could not receive the imperial crown because a woman was not eligible for imperial election.
politics.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: In 1784, Joseph II hoped to swap the Austrian Netherlands for the Electorate of Bavaria. As part of that deal he considered giving up the imperial title and granting it to the Elector of Bavaria, Charles Theodore. Already in 1778, he had pondered abdicating the title.
politics.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

politics.text: After the Thirty Years' War, the Kaiserliche Reichspost faced disputes over its authority, as mainly Protestant Imperial States of Northern Germany set up separate postal agencies. In the course of the War of the Spanish Succession, the Thurn und Taxis seat was relocated from Brussels to the Free City of Frankfurt in 1702.

philosophy.text: Kant's philosophy launched German idealism. In three major works, the Critique of Pure Reason (1781), Critique of Practical Reason (1788) and Critique of Judgment (1790), he set out to test the limits of rational thought. He called the result transcendental idealism.

German idealism is considered one of the most intellectually fertile periods in modern philosophy, with some comparing it to the golden age of philosophy in ancient Athens. Its most prominent figures were Kant, Fichte, Schelling and Hegel, the last considered the most influential.

German idealism grew out of Kant's attempt to reconcile the empiricism of David Hume with the rationalism of Leibniz and Spinoza. Hume's skepticism had argued that reason was subordinate to custom and habit. Kant's answer aimed to save the Enlightenment from that crisis.

At the Diet of Speyer in 1529, the Lutheran princes made their protestation, and at Augsburg in 1530 the Lutheran "Augsburg Confession" was rejected. A separate Lutheran church finally emerged. In 1529 Philipp Melanchthon had joined Luther in opposing a union with Zwingli.
philosophy.source_title: Germany in the early modern period

philosophy.text: In the 17th and 18th centuries, German cities became hubs of heretical and sometimes anti-religious freethinking. This challenged the influence of religion and helped spread secular thinking about morality across Germany and Europe.

In his 1784 essay "Answering the Question: What Is Enlightenment?", Kant argued that reason must first be subjected to a critique that establishes its proper boundaries. This required the courage to think for oneself rather than deferring to external authority. He hoped to establish criticism without skepticism, and naturalism without materialism.
The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 recognized the Lutheran faith in the Holy Roman Empire. It also stipulated that the religion of a state was to be that of its ruler, known as cuius regio, eius religio.

Emperor Rudolf II, who succeeded Maximilian II in 1576, preferred classical Greek philosophy to Christianity. He lived an isolated existence in Bohemia. He became afraid to act as the Catholic Church forcibly reasserted control in Austria and Hungary, upsetting Protestant princes.

Rationalist historians in the 18th century concluded that the use of torture had resulted in erroneous testimony in witch trials. Accused witches were tortured to force confessions and to make them name alleged co-conspirators, and the article says most historians agree the majority of those persecuted were innocent of any Devil worship.
philosophy.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period

culture.text: In 1517 Martin Luther published his Ninety-five Theses in Wittenberg, an event usually seen as the start of the Reformation. It divided the German states along religious lines. The north, the east and major cities such as Strasbourg, Frankfurt and Nuremberg became Protestant, while the south and west largely stayed Catholic. The Reformation brought unprecedented levels of violence and political upheaval to the region.
culture.source_title: Germany in the early modern period

culture.text: Between about 1400 and 1775, about 100,000 people were prosecuted for witchcraft in Europe and British America, and between 40,000 and 60,000 were executed, almost all in Europe. The witch hunts were particularly severe in parts of the Holy Roman Empire. Prosecutions peaked from 1560 to 1630, during the Counter-Reformation and the wars of religion. Roughly 80% of those convicted were women, most over the age of 40, and in some regions the convicted were burnt at the stake.
culture.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period

culture.text: Luther translated the Bible from Latin to German, which set the basis of the modern German language. Curiously, he spoke a dialect that had only minor importance at the time. After his Bible translation was published, that dialect evolved into what is now standard modern German.

From 1545 the Counter-Reformation began in Germany, driven largely by the Jesuit order, which had been founded in 1540. It restored Catholicism to many areas, including Bavaria. Southern Germany and the Rhineland largely remained Catholic, while northern and central Germany became mostly Lutheran or Calvinist.

Mass witch trials struck Southern Catholic Germany in waves between the 1560s and the 1620s. They included the Trier trials (1581-1593), the Fulda trials (1603-1606), the Eichstätt trials (1613-1630) and the Bamberg trials (1626-1631). Some ran for years and ended in hundreds of executions of both sexes, all ages and classes. The prince-bishops' lands were so hard hit that the contemporary writer Herman Löher called their subjects the most terrified people on earth.
culture.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period

culture.text: By the late 18th century, German intellectuals such as Johann Gottfried Herder articulated a German identity rooted in language. This idea helped spark the German nationalist movement. It arose after centuries of political fragmentation, when a sense of German unity began to emerge in the 18th century.

The Würzburg witch trials ran from 1626 to 1631 under Prince-Bishop Philipp Adolf von Ehrenberg. They led to the execution of about 900 people, and victims included nobles, councilmen and even children as young as seven. Torture was used to extract confessions and to make people name alleged accomplices, which caused a cycle of accusations and executions.
culture.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period

culture.text: When Francis I was made emperor in 1745, his wife Maria Theresa burst out laughing at the sight of him in his imperial coronation robes. She regarded the coronation as Kasperltheater, meaning a Punch and Judy show. She could not be elected herself because a woman was not eligible for the Imperial crown.
culture.source_title: Dissolution of the Holy Roman Empire

culture.text: The Würzburg witch trials of 1626 to 1631 were among the largest and deadliest in history. Under Prince-Bishop Philipp Adolf von Ehrenberg, about 900 people were executed, including nobles, councilmen and children as young as seven. Torture was used to extract confessions and to name alleged accomplices, which caused a cycle of accusations and executions.
culture.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period

culture.text: The Frisian island of Föhr was a stronghold of Dutch whaling personnel. In 1762, at the height of Dutch whaling, 1,186 seamen from Föhr served on Dutch whaling vessels alone, and 25% of all shipmasters on those vessels were from Föhr.

In south-western Germany between 1561 and 1670 there were 480 witch trials, 317 of them in Catholic areas and 163 in Protestant territories. At least 3,229 people were executed for witchcraft. Of these, 2,527 were tried and executed in Catholic territories and 702 in Protestant ones.
culture.source_title: Witch trials in the early modern period
